lessons.title: How a dairy cow uses feed
lessons.html:
The rumen

Cows are ruminants. Their rumen is a large fermentation vat where microbes break down fibre from grass, hay and silage. The microbes produce volatile fatty acids, which supply most of the cow's energy, and microbial protein, which the cow digests further down the gut. Feeding a dairy cow is really feeding her rumen microbes, and keeping the rumen stable is the first rule.

Nutrients a dairy cow needs

  • Water: milk is mostly water; a lactating cow drinks large volumes, more in hot weather. Clean water must always be available.
  • Energy: the main limit to milk yield in high producers; supplied by starch (maize, other grains) and digestible fibre.
  • Protein: for milk protein, growth and the rumen microbes; from pastures such as ryegrass and clover, oilcake meals and by-products.
  • Fibre: long, effective fibre keeps cows chewing the cud, produces saliva that buffers the rumen and supports butterfat.
  • Minerals and vitamins: calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, salt, trace elements and vitamins; supplied by licks or premixes.

Common South African feeds

TypeExamples
PastureKikuyu, ryegrass, clover, lucerne grazing
Conserved forageMaize silage, oat or ryegrass silage, lucerne hay, teff hay
Energy concentratesMaize meal, hominy chop
Protein concentratesSoybean oilcake, sunflower oilcake, cottonseed
Commercial dairy mealBalanced concentrate fed in the parlour or mixed

Rumen problems

Too much starch too fast, or too little effective fibre, causes rumen acidosis: cows go off feed, dung becomes loose, butterfat falls and lameness increases. Change rations gradually over days, not overnight, and never let cows gorge on grain. Follow the nutritionist's ration and mixing instructions.

lessons.title: Feeding management by stage and system
lessons.html:
Feeding through the lactation

StageFeeding focus
Early lactationHigh energy density, good protein, maximise intake; avoid acidosis
Mid and late lactationMatch feed to yield; regain body condition without overfattening
Far-off dryMainly roughage; maintain condition
Close-up dry (transition)Special ration as the nutritionist designs, to prepare the rumen and reduce milk fever and other metabolic disease

Pasture-based feeding

  • Allocate pasture by camp rotation so cows graze at the right growth stage and pastures can regrow.
  • Estimate pasture available and allocate a daily area per group.
  • Supplement with concentrate in the parlour and with silage or hay when pasture is short.
  • Watch for bloat on lush clover or lucerne; follow the farm's bloat prevention plan and call the vet urgently for bloated cows.

TMR feeding

  • Load ingredients in the mixer in the order and quantities on the mixing sheet; weigh accurately.
  • Mix for the set time; over-mixing chops fibre too short, under-mixing lets cows sort.
  • Push up feed regularly so it is always within reach.
  • Record refusals (leftovers) daily and adjust amounts; aim for a small amount left, not empty troughs.

Feed quality and storage

  • Silage must be well compacted and sealed; remove spoiled, mouldy silage before feeding.
  • Store concentrates dry and rodent-free; use first in, first out.
  • Do not feed mouldy feed; some moulds produce toxins harmful to cows and can pass into milk.

Feed efficiency

Feed is the biggest cost. Track feed cost per litre of milk and kilograms of milk per kilogram of dry matter eaten. Reduce waste at the bunker, in the mixer and in troughs.

Safety

Keep clear of mixer augers and power take-off shafts; never climb into a mixer unless it is switched off and locked out. Be careful on silage bunker faces, which can collapse.

Key points

  • Feed the rumen: keep enough effective fibre and change rations gradually.
  • Clean water must always be available.
  • Match feeding to lactation stage, with a special transition ration.
  • Manage pasture allocation and bloat risk; mix TMR accurately and record refusals.
  • Never feed mouldy feed; work safely around mixers and bunkers.
